Where exactly are the synergies coming from?

I have written headlines for a business newspaper for eleven years, and the job is mostly about deleting words. A reporter sends me a sentence like this: a company that is based in Brazil and makes packaging has agreed to be bought by a rival from the Netherlands for two point four billion dollars in cash. My job is to fit that into seven words. So the company that is based in Brazil becomes Brazil-based. The deal that is paid in cash becomes an all-cash deal. And the whole thing becomes: Brazilian packaging group agrees Dutch takeover. Readers who are new to English often find headlines harder than the article itself, and that is completely normal. The trick is to read the noun phrase from the right. The last noun is the thing. Everything in front of it is describing it. A packaging group takeover bid is a bid. Once you see that, the headline is just a very short story, and you can unpack it in your head before you even start the first paragraph.

In twenty years of mergers and acquisitions, I have learned that the day of the headline is the easiest day of the deal. Everybody is happy. The board has approved the offer, the shareholders are getting a premium, and the press release talks about synergies. Then the real work starts. First, there is regulatory approval. If the two companies together control too much of a market, the antitrust authorities can take a year to decide, and they can ask you to sell part of the business. Second, there is the integration. Two companies with two cultures, two computer systems and two sets of managers who all want the same job. Most of the synergies that were promised on day one depend on this part, and this is where many deals quietly fail. So when a client shows me a headline about a big takeover, my first question is never about the price. It is: how long until closing, and what has to happen before then?
